intro: For eleven units you have read other people's sacred texts: the Sabbath commandment in Exodus, the Sermon on the Mount, the opening sura of the Qur'an, Krishna's counsel to Arjuna, the Buddha's first teaching, the sayings of Confucius, the hymns of Guru Nanak, and stories told by elders of the Great Lakes and West Africa. In the last unit six students answered one question from six traditions. Now the question is yours. You will choose it, find the texts, and argue what three traditions would say.

This unit has two chapters. The first follows a student named Maya from a blank index card to a stack of quoted, cited and carefully read primary sources. You will learn to shrink a topic into a researchable question, to find reliable translations, to read with author, audience and purpose, to cite each scripture in its own system, and to avoid stereotype. The second chapter follows her to the front of the room, where she writes a thesis, builds layered evidence, compares without ranking, and answers questions from her classmates.

The capstone is not a test of what you believe. Students of every faith and of none do the same work on equal terms. It is a test of whether you can read what others hold sacred accurately and fairly, and report what you found in a way a thoughtful member of each tradition would recognize. By the end you will be able to pose a comparative question, gather and cite primary texts, and argue from them in writing and aloud.
bigQuestion: How can you let three traditions' own texts answer a question you care about, fairly, accurately and without ranking them?

Which religion forgives best?
Do Buddhists forgive?

Ramanuja's commentary on the Gita
The Sanskrit text of chapter 2
An encyclopedia summary of Hinduism

Summarize it loosely to save time

Skip the citation, since listeners cannot see it

Say all three views are identical

write.prompt: Choose a question about work, family, forgiveness, the natural world, wealth or war. Cite one primary text from each of three traditions studied in this course. Argue what each tradition would say and why, using the text, its context and how adherents read it, and end with a comparison that names both a parallel and a contrast.

Attribute every belief: according to the Torah, many Buddhists hold, in Sikh teaching.
Name the branch or school you mean, and report at least one disagreement within a tradition.
Compare rather than judge: show where the answers meet and where they part, without ranking.

title: Capstone: The Sources Speak

chapters.title: Posing the Question and Gathering the Texts
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you turn a question you actually care about into a fair, well-sourced study of what three traditions say?

story.title: The Question She Could Not Put Down
story.kicker: A senior has one week to pick a capstone question, and the one she wants has been waiting since the Hebrew Bible unit.
paragraphs: Maya sits in the back row with a blank index card. The assignment is simple to say and hard to do: choose one question, find what three religious traditions say about it in their own texts, and argue what each would answer and why. The teacher has written six starting topics on the board: work, family, forgiveness, the natural world, wealth, war. Most of the class is already writing. Maya is not.

Her problem is not that she has no question. It is that she has had one since October. In the unit on the Hebrew Bible the class read the Sabbath commandment from Exodus, the one that tells a household to stop working on the seventh day. Maya works twenty hours a week at a grocery store on Dempster Street. She has not had a full day off in months. She wrote in her notes that night: Why do so many traditions say that rest is holy, and does anyone still mean it?

That question is too big, and she knows it. It would take a lifetime. But inside it is a smaller one that a student can actually answer with texts: What does each tradition say a person owes to rest, and why? She remembers the class touching this in other units too. There was a line in the Gita about doing your duty without clinging to results. There was something in the Analects about a ruler who does not overwork the people. She is not sure she remembers either one correctly. That is the point of the next two weeks.

She writes on the card: Topic, work. Question, what does each tradition say a person owes to rest, and why? Traditions, Judaism, Hinduism, Confucianism. Under that she writes three more words: find the texts. This chapter is about what happens between that index card and a stack of quoted, cited, carefully read primary sources. The capstone is not a test of what you believe. It is a test of whether you can read what others hold sacred, accurately and fairly, and say what you found.
story.think: Maya's first question was too big and her second was answerable from texts. What is the difference between the two, and how would you shrink a question you care about?

lessons.title: What Makes a Question Researchable
lessons.mainIdea: A good capstone question is open, comparable across traditions, and answerable from primary texts.
reading: In the last unit six students stood at the board and answered one question with six traditions. The capstone reverses that. You choose the question, and the texts do the answering. A *researchable question* has three features. It is open, meaning it cannot be answered yes or no. It is comparable, meaning more than one tradition has actually spoken to it in its texts. And it is answerable from evidence, meaning you can point to a verse, a teaching or a practice rather than to your own opinion.

Test each feature against a real example. Is war ever right? is open, and nearly every tradition has texts about war, so it is comparable. But it is enormous. A student who asks it will drown in material. Compare it with a narrower version: What do the Torah, the Qur'an and the Dhammapada say about the treatment of an enemy? That question points to three specific texts and one specific issue. It is still open, still comparable, and now answerable in ten pages.

The six starting topics on the board, work, family, forgiveness, the natural world, wealth and war, were chosen because every tradition studied in this course has spoken to each of them. A *topic* is a subject area. A question is a sentence that ends with a question mark and demands evidence. Wealth is a topic. What does each tradition say a rich person owes to the poor, and why? is a question. Your first job is to move from the one to the other.

One more test matters in a public-school course. The question must be about what traditions teach, not about which one is right. Which religion has the best view of forgiveness? cannot be answered by any text, because the texts do not compete in a contest. How do three traditions explain why a person should forgive? can be answered, and answered well, because each tradition has given its reasons in writing. Keep the question descriptive and the whole project stays on solid ground.

words.d: a question that is open, that more than one tradition has addressed, and that can be answered from primary texts
a broad subject area, such as wealth or war, that is not yet a question
reporting what a tradition teaches without judging whether it is true

check.q: Which feature is required of a researchable capstone question?
choices: It can be answered from primary texts
It has one correct answer that all traditions share
It asks which tradition is most convincing
It can be answered yes or no
check.why: A researchable question is open, comparable and answerable from evidence such as a verse or a teaching, not from opinion.

check.q: What is the difference between a topic and a question in this project?
choices: A topic is about one tradition; a question is about three
A topic is a broad subject; a question is a sentence that demands evidence
A topic comes from the teacher; a question comes from a textbook
There is no difference; the words are interchangeable
check.why: Wealth is a topic. What does each tradition say a rich person owes the poor? is a question that asks for evidence.

check.q: Why does the lesson reject the question Which religion has the best view of forgiveness?
choices: Because forgiveness is not discussed in any sacred text
Because it is too narrow to fill ten pages
Because no text can answer which tradition is right; the project describes rather than ranks
Because only two traditions talk about forgiveness
check.why: The capstone is descriptive. Texts explain why a person should forgive; they do not compete in a contest that a student can judge.

lessons.title: Narrowing a Topic to a Question
lessons.mainIdea: Shrink a topic step by step until the question names one issue that three traditions have addressed in texts.
reading: Start with wealth. It is a fine topic and a hopeless question. Ask what about wealth actually puzzles you. Maybe it is this: some people in every tradition are rich, and every tradition seems to say something uneasy about riches. That is a real observation, and it can be turned into a question in stages. Stage one: What do religions say about wealth? Still too big. Stage two: What do traditions say a wealthy person should do with money? Better. Stage three: What do the Hebrew prophets, the Gospels and the Qur'an say a wealthy person owes to the poor, and why? Now you have a question.

Notice what changed at each stage. The word religions became three named traditions. The vague say about became owes to the poor, one specific duty. And the question gained a why, which forces you to look for the reasons a text gives, not just its rule. A rule without its reason tells you little. Deuteronomy commands leaving the forgotten sheaf and the gleanings of the harvest for the stranger, the orphan and the widow, and explains that Israel was once enslaved in Egypt. The Qur'an makes *zakat*, the required giving of a share of wealth, one of the Five Pillars and ties it to purifying what one keeps. The reasons are where the traditions differ most, and where your paper gets interesting.

Here is the same process on family. Stage one: What do religions teach about family? Stage two: What do traditions teach that children owe to parents? Stage three: How do the Ten Commandments, the Analects and the Guru Granth Sahib describe what a grown child owes to aging parents? The last version is *narrow* enough to answer because it names an age, a duty and three texts. The Analects speak at length of *xiao*, often translated as filial piety, the respect and care a child owes to parents. The commandment to honor father and mother sits in Exodus 20. Sikh teaching includes service to family as part of an honest householder's life.

A warning about narrowing too far. What does the Qur'an say in sura 2, verse 177? is narrow, but it is not a question you can compare across traditions. Stop narrowing when the question names one issue, asks for reasons, and can still be put to three traditions. Write the final version at the top of your notes and check every source you gather against it. If a source does not help answer that exact question, it goes in a separate pile for later, not in the paper.

words.d: to make a question more specific by naming the issue, the duty and the texts it is about
in Islam, the required giving of a set share of one's wealth each year; one of the Five Pillars
in Confucian teaching, filial piety: the respect, obedience and care a child owes to parents

look.title: From the Natural World to a Question
look.text: Stage one: What do religions say about nature? Stage two: What do traditions say humans owe to the land and to animals? Stage three: How do Genesis, the Jain vows and an Ojibwe teaching about the land describe what humans owe to other living things, and why? At each stage, something vague became something named.
look.prompt: Take the topic war through the same three stages. Write all three versions, and underline what became more specific each time.

check.q: In the wealth example, what did adding the word why to the question accomplish?
choices: It made the question about only one tradition
It turned the question into a yes-or-no question
It removed the need to quote any text
It forced the student to look for each text's reasons, not just its rule
check.why: A rule without its reason tells you little. The reasons are where traditions differ most, so the why makes the comparison possible.

check.q: Which version of the family question is narrow enough to research?
choices: How do the Ten Commandments, the Analects and the Guru Granth Sahib describe what a grown child owes to aging parents?
What do religions teach about family?
Is family important in religion?
What do traditions say about people?
check.why: It names an age, a duty and three texts while still asking for reasons and staying comparable.

check.q: Why is What does the Qur'an say in sura 2, verse 177? too narrow for the capstone?
choices: Because the Qur'an cannot be quoted in a school paper
Because it names one verse in one tradition and cannot be compared across three
Because verse numbers are not used in Islamic texts
Because it asks for a reason instead of a rule
check.why: A capstone question must still be put to three traditions. A single verse in a single text is a source, not a comparative question.

lessons.title: Choosing Three Traditions
lessons.mainIdea: Pick three traditions that have each spoken to your question in their texts, and choose for range rather than for convenience.
reading: Three is the number for a reason. One tradition gives you a report, not a comparison. Two invite a contest, this one versus that one. Three make a conversation, in which you can see two traditions agree while a third answers differently, and then ask why. The course has covered the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament, Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism, Daoism, Sikhism, Jainism, and the oral traditions of West Africa and Native North America. Any three that have addressed your question will work.

Choose for *range*. If all three of your traditions are Abrahamic, meaning they trace their story through Abraham, as Judaism, Christianity and Islam do, you will find many shared ideas and fewer surprises. Many strong papers pair one Abrahamic tradition with one tradition from India, such as Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism or Sikhism, and one from East Asia or from the oral traditions. On the question of rest, for example, the Sabbath, the Buddhist monastic day and the Daoist idea of *wu wei*, acting without forcing, give three very different answers to why a person should stop.

Check that each tradition has texts on your question before you commit. Some pairings look promising and turn out thin. A question about a written code of law will find rich material in the Torah, the Qur'an and the Analects, but an Ojibwe oral tradition does not keep its teaching in that form, and forcing it into a law-code comparison would misrepresent it. A question about what humans owe the land runs the other way: Native traditions of the Great Lakes have much to say, and you would be wise to include one, using sources the community itself has chosen to make public.

Size is not the test. Christianity has about 2.4 billion adherents by common estimates and Jainism perhaps four to five million, but a Jain text on nonviolence may answer a question about war more sharply than any larger tradition. Nor should you choose a tradition because you already belong to it or already dislike it. The teacher will ask you to name your three traditions and one text from each before you go further, which is a check that you have looked and not guessed.

words.d: variety among the traditions chosen, so that the comparison shows real differences
describing Judaism, Christianity and Islam, which each trace their story through Abraham
in Daoist teaching, acting without forcing or striving; effortless action in harmony with the Dao

Because three make a conversation in which two may agree and a third answer differently
Because the rubric gives extra points for each tradition
Because only three traditions were studied in the course

check.q: Which set of three traditions shows the most range?
choices: Judaism, Christianity and Islam
Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christianity
Islam, Buddhism and an Ojibwe tradition
Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism
check.why: That set draws on an Abrahamic tradition, an Indian tradition and an oral tradition of the Great Lakes. The others stay within one family.

check.q: Why might a question about written law codes be a poor fit for an Ojibwe oral tradition?
choices: Because Ojibwe people have no teachings about right conduct
Because oral traditions are not allowed in school papers
Because the Ojibwe tradition is too small to compare
Because the tradition does not keep its teaching as a written code, so the comparison would misrepresent it
check.why: The lesson warns that forcing an oral tradition into a law-code comparison distorts it. Choose questions each tradition has actually addressed in its own form.

lessons.title: Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Sources
lessons.mainIdea: A primary source is the tradition's own text; a secondary source explains it; a tertiary source summarizes the explanations.
reading: Open three tabs. In the first is Psalm 23 in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation. In the second is a rabbi's essay on what the psalm meant to shepherds in ancient Judah. In the third is an encyclopedia entry titled Psalms. These are three kinds of source, and the capstone treats them differently. The psalm is a *primary source*: the text itself, as the tradition preserves it. The essay is a *secondary source*: a scholar or adherent interpreting the text. The encyclopedia entry is a *tertiary source*: a summary of what secondary sources generally say.

The rule for the capstone is that every claim about what a tradition teaches rests on at least one primary source, quoted and cited. Secondary sources help you understand the primary text and tell you how adherents read it, and you should use them. Tertiary sources are for orientation only. They can point you to the right chapter of the Qur'an or the right book of the Analects, but they are not evidence, and a paper built on encyclopedia entries will read like one.

Primary sources come in more forms than you might expect. For Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, Confucianism and Daoism there are written scriptures with chapters and verses. For Jainism there are the Agamas and the writings of later teachers. For the oral traditions of West Africa and Native North America, the primary source may be a story, a song or a ceremony as told by an authorized speaker, and it may exist only in a recording or a transcription the community approved. A transcription of an elder telling a creation story is a primary source; a professor's book about creation stories is secondary.

Be careful with one common trap. A modern religious leader's sermon quoting a verse is a secondary source about the verse, even though it is a primary source about that leader's views. If your question is what the Gospels say about wealth, cite the Gospel. If your question is how twenty-first-century preachers in Chicago read the Gospel on wealth, the sermon becomes your primary source. Which kind of source a document is depends on the question you are asking of it.

words.d: the tradition's own text, story or ceremony, as it preserves it, such as a verse of the Qur'an or a psalm
a scholar's or adherent's interpretation of a primary text, such as a commentary or essay
a summary of secondary sources, such as an encyclopedia entry or a textbook overview

They replace the need to quote primary texts
They orient the student and point toward the right chapter, but are not evidence

lessons.title: Public-Domain Translations and Their Limits
lessons.mainIdea: Public-domain translations can be quoted freely, but each carries the language and assumptions of its own century.
reading: This course quotes a specific set of English translations word for word because they are in the *public domain*, meaning their copyright has expired and anyone may reproduce them. The King James Bible of 1611; the Jewish Publication Society Tanakh of 1917; J. M. Rodwell's Qur'an of 1861 and E. H. Palmer's of 1880; Max Müller's Sacred Books of the East, fifty volumes published from 1879 to 1910, which include the Dhammapada, the Upanishads and the Daodejing; James Legge's Analects of 1861; Edwin Arnold's verse Bhagavad Gita of 1885; and Max Arthur Macauliffe's six-volume work on the Sikh Gurus of 1909. You may quote any of these exactly.

Each of them is also old, and age has costs. The King James Bible uses thee and thou and words whose meanings have shifted. Rodwell rearranged the Qur'an's chapters into what he guessed was chronological order, which no Muslim edition does, so his chapter numbers can mislead. Müller and Legge were Victorian scholars who sometimes described the traditions they translated as inferior to Christianity, and those attitudes leak into footnotes and introductions. Arnold turned the Gita into English poetry and added words for the sake of rhythm. Macauliffe was more sympathetic, working closely with Sikh scholars, but his English is formal and his volumes mix translation with retelling.

Modern translations are usually clearer and often more accurate, and you should read them. Most are under copyright, so you may quote only short passages with citation, which is normal academic practice, and you must say whose translation you are using. Better still, read your key verse in two translations, one old and one modern, and note where they differ. A difference between translations is not a problem to hide. It is evidence about the text, and a paragraph explaining it shows a reader that you understand every translation is an *interpretation*.

For traditions without a single scripture, translation raises a different problem. A Yoruba praise poem for an orisha, or an Ojibwe teaching about the land, was translated by someone, and that someone may have been an outsider with limited understanding. Prefer versions produced by or with the community itself, and say who produced them. When you cannot find a reliable version, say that too. Honest limits are part of good research.

words.d: works whose copyright has expired, so anyone may copy and quote them freely
an explanation of what a text means; every translation is one, because it makes choices about words
a fifty-volume series of English translations of Asian religious texts edited by Max Müller, 1879 to 1910

look.title: When the Public-Domain Translations Appeared
look.cite: Publication dates of the translations named in the course
look.prompt: The newest of these is more than a century old. Name two specific costs of that age that the lesson describes, and one reason the course still uses them.

check.q: Why does the course quote the King James Bible and Müller's Dhammapada word for word?
choices: Because they are the most accurate translations available
Because adherents of every tradition prefer them
Because they were written by members of each tradition
Because they are in the public domain and may be reproduced freely

check.q: What problem does the lesson raise about Rodwell's 1861 Qur'an?
choices: He rearranged the chapters into a guessed chronological order that no Muslim edition uses
He translated only half of the text
He wrote it in verse and added words for rhythm
He worked from a Latin translation rather than Arabic
check.why: Rodwell reordered the suras, so his chapter numbers can mislead a student comparing with a standard edition.

choices: Choose the older one, since it is public domain
Leave the verse out of the paper
Explain the difference, because it is evidence about the text
Average the two into a new wording
check.why: A difference between translations is evidence, and explaining it shows the reader that every translation is an interpretation.

lessons.title: Where Reliable Texts Live
lessons.mainIdea: Find primary texts through libraries, universities, museums and the traditions' own publishers, and judge every website by who made it and why.
reading: A search engine will return a verse of the Qur'an in a tenth of a second, and it may be wrong. It may be mistranslated, misnumbered, cut short or posted by a group hostile to Islam. The capstone asks you to know where your text came from. Start with the school and public library. Librarians can pull complete printed editions of every scripture in this course, along with scholarly commentaries. The Chicago Public Library and suburban systems such as Skokie's hold many of them, and the Newberry Library downtown keeps rare early editions that you can request to see.

Online, prefer sites that show their sources. University digital libraries post scanned copies of the Sacred Books of the East and the 1917 JPS Tanakh with page images, so you can check the printed text yourself. Major museums, including the Art Institute of Chicago and the Field Museum, publish catalog entries for manuscripts and ritual objects with expert descriptions. Religious communities publish their own scriptures: many Sikh gurdwaras link to searchable editions of the Guru Granth Sahib with the page number, called the *ang*, beside every line. A tradition's own edition tells you how the community itself presents the text.

Judge a website the way you judge any source: author, audience, purpose. Who made it, and what do they know? For whom, and in what tone? Why does it exist? A site run by a seminary, a university department or a religious body has a clear author and purpose. An anonymous page with no dates and heavy advertising has neither. Be especially careful with sites that quote another tradition's text only to attack it. A page of Qur'an verses assembled to prove Islam violent, or of Bible verses assembled to prove Christianity absurd, is not a source for what the tradition teaches. It is a source for what its author thinks, and it belongs in a different paper.

Keep a *source log* from the first day. For each text write the title, the translator, the year, the edition or website, the date you looked at it and the exact location of the passage. If it is a website, save the address and a copy of the page. You will need all of this for your citations, and you will be surprised how quickly you forget where a good quote came from. A log also lets a reader, or a teacher, retrace your steps, which is what makes research *verifiable*.

words.d: the word Sikhs use for a page of the Guru Granth Sahib; the scripture has 1,430 angs in its standard edition
a running record of every text consulted, with translator, year, edition, location and date accessed
able to be checked by another person retracing the same sources

lessons.title: Author, Audience and Purpose Again
lessons.mainIdea: Before a verse can count as evidence, ask who is speaking in it, to whom, and for what purpose.
reading: The first unit of this course gave you a toolkit: author, audience, purpose. The capstone is where it earns its keep. Take a verse that students often choose for questions about justice, Micah 6:8 in the Hebrew Bible. In the King James translation the prophet says that God has shown what is good: to do justly, love mercy and walk humbly. Before you quote it, run the toolkit. The *author*, as the tradition presents it, is a prophet named Micah, speaking in the kingdom of Judah in the eighth century BCE. The audience is his own people, whom the surrounding chapters accuse of cheating the poor. The purpose is to correct them: sacrifices without justice, he argues, are not what God wants.

Now the verse means more, and it means something more specific. It is not a general saying about being nice. It is a prophet's answer to people who thought ritual could replace fairness. A paper that quotes Micah 6:8 and then explains that setting shows the reader that the student understands the text. A paper that quotes it as a free-floating motto does not. The same three questions work on every text in this course. Who speaks in the Gita? Krishna, to Arjuna, on a battlefield, to a warrior who has lost his nerve. Who speaks in the Analects? Usually Confucius, to named students, answering their questions about conduct and government.

Author is the hardest of the three, because traditions and scholars often answer it differently, and you must report both. Jewish and Christian tradition long attributed the Torah to Moses; most academic scholars describe it as compiled from several sources over centuries. Muslims hold that the Qur'an is the word of God revealed to Muhammad; academic study describes its collection into a written text in the decades after his death in 632. Neither of these is your claim to settle. Write both, attribute each, and move on. The rubric rewards accuracy about what people hold, not a verdict.

Purpose is where students most often go wrong, because it requires reading around the verse. A single line can look like a command when it is part of a story, or like a promise when it is part of a warning. Before you copy any quotation into your notes, read at least the whole paragraph or the whole chapter it sits in, and write one sentence about what that larger passage is trying to do. That sentence will end up in your paper, and it is the difference between quoting a text and understanding it.

words.d: the speaker or writer of a text as the tradition presents it, and as scholars describe it; report both when they differ
in the Hebrew Bible, a person understood to speak a message from God, often calling the people back to justice
to name whose belief or claim a statement is, as in Muslims hold or Jewish tradition teaches

lessons.title: Genre Changes the Meaning
lessons.mainIdea: Law, story, poetry, prophecy, letter and teaching each ask to be read differently, and a paper should say which kind of text it is quoting.
reading: Two texts about rest. The first is a law: the Sabbath commandment in Exodus 20, counted fourth in Jewish and most Protestant numbering and third by Catholics and Lutherans, which orders a household, including servants, animals and foreigners living among them, to stop work on the seventh day. The second is a verse of teaching: the first line of the Dhammapada, which says that everything we are results from what we have thought. Both bear on a question about work and rest. But one is a *commandment*, given as binding law to a people, and the other is a *verse of teaching*, offered to anyone who will consider it. Quoting them as if they were the same kind of sentence would mislead your reader.

*Genre* is the kind of writing a text is. The first unit listed the main genres in sacred texts: law, story, poetry, prophecy, letter and teaching. Each asks for a different reading. A law tells you what a community was obligated to do, and often why. A story shows a value in action, through characters, without stating a rule. Poetry, like the Psalms or many hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib, expresses feeling and praise, and reading it as law produces nonsense. Prophecy calls a people back to something. A letter, like Paul's to the Corinthians, answers particular problems in a particular town. Teaching, like the Analects or the Dhammapada, offers wisdom for a student to practice.

The Sabbath law has a reason built in. Exodus grounds it in creation: God rested on the seventh day. The parallel version in Deuteronomy 5 grounds it in memory: you were slaves in Egypt, and now your servants must rest too. That is two reasons from two passages of law, and a careful paper notes both. The Dhammapada's verse belongs to a different genre and a different logic. It does not order rest. It describes how the mind works, so that a reader will choose to train it. When Maya compares them in her capstone, she must say: one tradition frames rest as commanded, the other frames the quieting of the mind as chosen. Genre is not a detail. It is part of the answer.

In your notes, write the genre next to every quotation: law, story, poem, prophecy, letter, teaching, or, for oral traditions, story, song or ceremony. When you write the paper, name it in the sentence that introduces the quote. In the Torah's law of the Sabbath, Exodus commands. In a verse of teaching, the Dhammapada observes. In a parable, Jesus tells of. Those small phrases tell your reader you know what kind of text you are holding.

words.d: the kind of writing a text is, such as law, story, poetry, prophecy, letter or teaching
a binding instruction given as law; the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5 are the best-known example
a short saying offered for a student to consider and practice, as in the Dhammapada or the Analects

lessons.title: How Adherents Read It
lessons.mainIdea: A text means what its community has understood it to mean, so report how adherents read a passage, not only what the words say.
reading: Leviticus 19:18 tells the Israelites not to take vengeance or bear a grudge, but to love their neighbor as themselves. A student could quote that verse and stop. A stronger student asks how the tradition has read it. In Jewish tradition the great teacher Hillel, around the turn of the first century, is remembered as saying that a version of this principle was the whole Torah and the rest was commentary. Rabbi Akiva in the second century called the verse a great principle of the Torah. Christians read the same verse through the Gospels, where Jesus quotes it as the second of the two greatest commandments. Same words, two communities, two readings, and both belong in a paper about what the verse means.

Every tradition in this course has an *interpretive tradition*, a long conversation about what its texts mean. Jews have the Talmud and the commentaries of Rashi and later rabbis. Christians have church councils, the writings of theologians and, in each denomination, a way of preaching. Muslims have *tafsir*, the discipline of Qur'an commentary, and the schools of law that draw rules from the text. Hindus have commentaries on the Gita by teachers such as Shankara, who read it as a text about knowledge, and Ramanuja, who read it as a text about devotion. Buddhists have commentaries in Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan. Sikhs have the tradition of *katha*, spoken exposition of the Guru Granth Sahib in the gurdwara.

For your paper this means one thing: never write the Qur'an says or the Gita teaches and stop there. Add how the tradition has taken it. Many Muslim scholars have read this verse as. Most Hindu teachers in the devotional tradition understand this passage as. When the tradition disagrees with itself, say so; that is not a weakness in your paper but a strength. If Shankara and Ramanuja read the same chapter differently, a reader learns that Hinduism is a family of paths, which is exactly what the Hinduism unit taught.

Where do you find how adherents read a text? In secondary sources written by members and scholars of the tradition, in the introductions to good modern translations, and, with your teacher's guidance, in a respectful visit or interview. Chicago's houses of worship have long welcomed students who come to learn rather than to argue. Write down who told you what, and treat a living person's words with the same care you give a written source. An interview is a source with an author, an audience and a purpose, like any other.

words.d: a community's long conversation about what its texts mean, carried in commentaries, councils, sermons and teaching
the Islamic discipline of Qur'an commentary; a tafsir is a written work explaining the Qur'an verse by verse
in Sikh practice, spoken exposition of the Guru Granth Sahib, usually in the gurdwara

lessons.title: How to Cite a Sacred Text
lessons.mainIdea: Each scripture has its own citation system, and a paper must use the right one so a reader can find the passage.
reading: A *citation* is the address of a passage. It lets a reader open the same text to the same place. Sacred texts have their own addressing systems that are older than page numbers, and using them correctly is a mark of care. The Hebrew Bible and the New Testament are cited by book, chapter and verse, with a colon between chapter and verse: Micah 6:8, Matthew 5:9. A range uses a dash: Exodus 20:8-11. Then name the translation: Micah 6:8, King James Version, or Micah 6:8, JPS 1917. The Jewish Bible and Christian Bibles number a few verses differently, so check which numbering your edition uses.

The Qur'an is cited by *sura*, meaning chapter, and *ayah*, meaning verse: Qur'an 2:177 or, in words, sura 2, verse 177. There are 114 suras, and each has a name as well as a number, such as al-Baqara, The Cow, for sura 2. Because Rodwell rearranged the suras, always cite the standard numbering and note if you are quoting his translation. The Dhammapada is cited by verse, sometimes with the chapter: Dhammapada 5, or Dhammapada, chapter 1, verse 5. The Bhagavad Gita is cited by chapter and verse, 2.47, and note that it sits inside book 6 of the Mahabharata, a fact you need not include in the citation.

The Analects are cited by book and chapter, 15.23 or XV.23, though numbering varies slightly between editions, so name the translator. The Daodejing is cited by chapter, 1 through 81. The Guru Granth Sahib is cited by ang, the page number in the standard 1,430-page edition, and often by the composer, since the scripture gathers hymns of six Gurus and of Hindu and Muslim saints. A citation reads: Guru Granth Sahib, ang 1, Guru Nanak. The Talmud is cited by tractate and folio with a side letter, such as Shabbat 31a. For oral traditions, cite the speaker, the community, the occasion and the recording or publication, and the permission under which it was shared.

Two rules cover every case. First, cite the exact location, not just the book. Second, name the translation or edition every time, because the words you quote are that translator's words. Build a citation list at the end of your paper that gives the full information for each translation once, and then use the short address in the text. When you paraphrase instead of quoting, cite anyway. The idea still came from the passage, and a reader deserves to check it.

words.d: the address of a passage, such as book, chapter and verse, plus the translation, so a reader can find it
a chapter of the Qur'an; there are 114, each with a number and a name
a verse of the Qur'an; the word also means a sign
one of the sections of the Talmud, cited with a folio number and side, as in Shabbat 31a

lessons.title: A Note System That Works
lessons.mainIdea: Take notes in three columns, the text, its context, and how adherents read it, tagged by tradition and tied to your question.
reading: Students lose more time to bad notes than to bad reading. A quotation copied without its citation is useless a week later. A good idea written on a loose page vanishes. The capstone asks for a simple, disciplined *note system* that you can search. Use index cards, a notebook or a document, but use the same format for every entry. At the top: the tradition and the citation. Below that, three columns or three short sections. First, the text, quoted exactly, with the translator named. Second, the context, meaning genre, speaker, audience and purpose in a sentence or two. Third, the reading, meaning how adherents and scholars have understood the passage, with the name of the secondary source.

Add a fourth line that many students skip: how this passage answers your question. Write it as a sentence, not a phrase. On Maya's card for Exodus 20:8-10 it might read: The Torah frames rest as a command binding on the whole household, grounded in God's own rest at creation, so in Jewish tradition rest is an obligation rather than a reward. That one sentence is a draft of a sentence in her paper. Twenty cards like it, and the paper is half written before she opens a blank document.

Tag every card by tradition and by *subquestion*. If your question is what a wealthy person owes the poor and why, your subquestions might be: who must give, how much, to whom, and for what reason. Tag each card with the subquestions it answers. When you sort by tag, you will see instantly that you have four cards on how much and none on why for one tradition, which tells you exactly what to read next. Gaps found in week one are easy to fill. Gaps found the night before are not.

Keep quotations and your own words visibly separate. Put every quoted phrase in quotation marks on the card, even a phrase of three words, and mark your paraphrases with a P. This protects you from *plagiarism*, presenting another's words or ideas as your own, which in this project would most often happen by accident, when a phrase from a commentary slides into your paragraph without a mark. It also protects the text. A sacred text quoted slightly wrong is a text misrepresented, and members of that tradition who read your paper will notice.

words.d: a fixed format for every research note: citation, exact text, context, adherents' reading, and how it answers the question
one of the smaller questions inside the main question, used to tag and sort notes
presenting another person's words or ideas as your own, whether on purpose or by accident

lessons.title: Avoiding Stereotype and Overgeneralization
lessons.mainIdea: Write about traditions with precise qualifiers, name the branch or school you mean, and never let one text or one adherent stand for everyone.
reading: The most common error in student papers about religion is a small word: all. All Muslims believe. All Buddhists meditate. All Christians read the Bible literally. Each of these is false, and each is a *stereotype*, a fixed idea applied to every member of a group. Islam has Sunni and Shia branches and many schools of law and thought within each. Most Buddhists worldwide do not practice sitting meditation daily; it has historically been a monastic discipline. Christians read the Bible in many ways, and the largest church, the Roman Catholic Church, does not teach a literal reading of every passage. A paper with all in it announces that its author has not looked closely.

The fix is precision, not vagueness. Replace all with a qualifier that matches your evidence: many, most, some, traditionally, in this school, according to this text. Then name the branch. Not Jews believe but in Orthodox Jewish practice, or Reform Judaism teaches. Not Buddhists hold but in the Theravada tradition, or in Zen. Not Hindus think but in the devotional path centered on Vishnu, or according to the Upanishads. Each of those phrases is true of a real group and can be checked. *Overgeneralization*, stretching a claim beyond the evidence that supports it, is what happens when the qualifier is missing.

One text is not the whole tradition, and one adherent is not either. If you interview a Sikh classmate, you have learned what one Sikh thinks, which is valuable and should be reported as exactly that. If you quote one verse from the Qur'an on war, you have one verse, and the Qur'an has others, and Muslim scholars have argued for fourteen centuries about how they fit together. Say so. The Qur'an itself speaks of humanity being made into nations and tribes so they might know one another, a verse many Muslims cite as a charter for diversity, and a student who quotes a verse on fighting without also noting that one has told half a story.

Watch for the historical version of the same mistake. Christianity did not always look like your neighborhood church, and Buddhism in fifth-century India is not Buddhism in Chicago today. Date your claims. The Sabbath command in Exodus is ancient; the rule that a Sabbath elevator stops on every floor is a modern Orthodox practice built from it. Both are Jewish, and both belong in a paper, but they belong with their dates. Precision about who, which branch and when is what turns a report about religion into scholarship about it.

words.d: a fixed, oversimplified idea applied to every member of a group
stretching a claim beyond the evidence that supports it, as when one text or one person is made to speak for a whole tradition
a word such as many, most, some or traditionally that limits a claim to what the evidence supports

review.why: Micah speaks to his own people, accused of cheating the poor, and argues that sacrifices without justice are not what God wants.

choices: The building of the Temple
The crossing of the Jordan
The covenant with Abraham
The memory of slavery in Egypt
review.why: Deuteronomy's version reminds the people that they were slaves, so their servants must rest too.

review.q: Shankara read the Gita as a text about knowledge and Ramanuja as a text about devotion. This is an example of what?
choices: An interpretive tradition disagreeing within itself
A translation error
A tertiary source
A stereotype

choices: All Christians read the Bible literally
Many Orthodox Jews observe the Sabbath by not switching electrical devices on or off
Buddhists do not believe in anything
Every Hindu worships Vishnu

chapters.title: Arguing What Each Would Say
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you argue what three traditions would say about a question, using their own texts, without ranking them or flattening them into one?

story.title: Three Texts and One Answer
story.kicker: Maya stands at the front of the room with three quotations, one thesis and nine minutes.
paragraphs: Two weeks after the blank index card, Maya has twenty-six note cards held together with a binder clip. Each one has a citation at the top, an exact quotation, a line about context and a line about how the tradition reads the passage. Her question has not changed: what does each tradition say a person owes to rest, and why? What has changed is that she can now answer it. On the screen behind her, the first slide shows three short passages side by side, each with its source underneath.

The first is from Exodus 20, the Sabbath commandment, in the King James translation. The second is a paraphrase of the Bhagavad Gita, chapter 6, where Krishna tells Arjuna that discipline is not for the person who sleeps too much or too little, but for the one who is moderate in eating, rest, work, sleep and waking. The third is a paraphrase of Analects 1.5, where Confucius says a good ruler employs the people only at the proper seasons. Three kinds of text: a law, a teaching given in a story, and a saying recorded by students.

Maya reads her thesis aloud. Each tradition says a person is owed rest, she argues, but each places that duty somewhere different. The Torah places it in God's command to a whole household, servants and animals included. The Gita places it in the balance of a disciplined self. The Analects place it in the virtue of a ruler who does not wear out the people. A classmate in the second row writes the three places down. That is what a thesis is for: it gives a listener something to hold.

Then come the questions. Does every Jewish family keep the Sabbath the way Exodus describes? Maya says no, and names the differences among Orthodox, Conservative and Reform practice. Isn't the Gita really about a war? Yes, she says, and explains that the teaching on balance is given on a battlefield, and that commentators have read that setting in different ways. Which view do you agree with? She smiles and says the assignment asked what each tradition would say, and that her answer is on the slide. This chapter follows the path from her note cards to that answer.
story.think: Maya declined to say which view she agreed with. Why might a presenter in a public-school course on religion make that choice, and what did she offer instead?

lessons.title: What a Thesis Claims
lessons.mainIdea: A capstone thesis states what each tradition would answer, names the reason each gives, and makes a comparison a reader could test against the texts.
reading: Maya's first draft of a thesis read: Judaism, Hinduism and Confucianism all value rest. Every word of it is true, and it says almost nothing. A *thesis* is the central claim of a paper, the one or two sentences the rest of the paper must prove. A weak thesis lists topics. A strong thesis argues. Her revised version reads: Each tradition says a person is owed rest, but each places that duty in a different spot: the Torah in God's command to the household, the Gita in the balance of a disciplined self, and the Analects in the virtue of a ruler.

The revision works because it has three parts. First, it answers the question for each tradition. Second, it names where each tradition grounds its answer, which is the why. Third, it makes a comparison: the same duty, located in three different places. It is also *arguable*, meaning a careful reader could disagree and would need evidence to settle the matter. Someone might say the Gita cares less about rest than about duty. Maya's paper must show, with the text, why balance is the right word.

Notice the phrase would say. The Torah, the Gita and the Analects were written long before anyone worked twenty hours a week at a grocery store. None of them answers Maya's question directly. So the capstone asks you to reason from what a text does say to what its tradition would likely answer. That reasoning must be visible. Each part of the thesis is a *claim*, and each claim must point to a passage. If the clause about the Gita cannot be tied to a verse, it must be cut or rewritten.

Three thesis mistakes are common. The ranking thesis says one tradition has the healthiest or most advanced view, which no text can prove and which the course does not ask. The sameness thesis says all religions teach the same thing about rest, which erases the differences adherents care about. The lopsided thesis gives one tradition a full answer and the other two a phrase each. The fix for all three is the same: one clear clause per tradition, one grounding per clause, and one sentence that compares them.

words.d: the central claim of a paper, stated in one or two sentences, that the rest of the paper sets out to prove
open to reasonable disagreement, so that evidence is needed to support it
a statement the writer asserts and must support with evidence, such as what a tradition teaches and why

look.title: Balance in the Gita
look.text: Krishna tells Arjuna that the discipline of yoga is not for one who eats too much or fasts too much, nor for one who sleeps too much or stays awake too long. For the person who is moderate in food and recreation, in effort at work, and in sleeping and waking, this discipline takes away sorrow.
look.prompt: Which clause of Maya's thesis does this passage support? Write the one sentence that connects the passage to the clause.

check.q: Why was Maya's first draft, Judaism, Hinduism and Confucianism all value rest, a weak thesis?
choices: It named the traditions but made no argument about why or how they differ
It contained a factual error about Judaism
It ranked the three traditions
It was too long for one sentence
check.why: A weak thesis lists topics. The revision names where each tradition grounds rest and compares them, which is an argument.

check.q: What does the phrase would say ask the student to do?
choices: Report what adherents said in interviews only
Guess freely about a tradition's views
Reason from what a text does say to what its tradition would likely answer, showing the reasoning
Quote a text that answers the modern question word for word
check.why: Ancient texts do not answer modern questions directly, so the student reasons from the passage and makes each step visible.

check.q: Which thesis makes the sameness mistake?
choices: Judaism has the healthiest view of rest
The Torah grounds rest in command, the Gita in balance, and the Analects in a ruler's virtue
The Gita gives the fullest answer, and the other two add a little
All religions teach the same thing about rest
check.why: The sameness thesis erases differences that adherents care about. The first choice ranks, and the third is lopsided.

lessons.title: Evidence in Three Layers
lessons.mainIdea: Strong evidence has three layers, the quoted text, its context and how adherents have read it, joined to the claim by a sentence of reasoning.
reading: In the Torah's law, the Sabbath commandment of Exodus 20 tells a household to stop work on the seventh day. That quotation is the first layer of *evidence*, the text itself. By itself it proves little, because a reader does not yet know what kind of text it is or how anyone has lived by it. A paragraph that drops a quotation and moves on leaves the reader to do the work. The capstone asks you to do that work on the page.

The second layer is *context*: genre, speaker, audience and setting. Exodus 20 is law, presented as given to Israel at Mount Sinai. It names who must rest: children, servants, animals and the foreigner living among the people. Deuteronomy 5 repeats the command and adds a reason, the memory of slavery in Egypt. The third layer is the reading of the community. The Mishnah, the early rabbinic law code compiled about 200 CE, lists thirty-nine categories of forbidden work, called *melakhot*. Rabbinic law also holds that saving a life overrides the Sabbath.

The three layers still need a sentence that joins them to the claim. That sentence is the *warrant*, the reasoning that explains why this evidence supports this claim. Maya writes: Because the commandment lists servants, animals and strangers, and because Deuteronomy ties it to the memory of slavery, the Torah treats rest as something owed to the vulnerable, not only chosen by the free. Without that sentence, a reader sees a verse and a claim sitting side by side, and has to guess how they connect.

Every body paragraph in the capstone can follow the same order. State the claim. Quote the text with its citation. Give the context in a sentence or two. Report how adherents have read it, naming the source. Write the warrant. Five moves, in that order, turn a quotation into an argument. It feels slow at first. By the third tradition it becomes a habit, and a reader can follow every step you took.

words.d: the material that supports a claim; in the capstone, a quoted text together with its context and its reading
the genre, speaker, audience and setting of a passage, which shape what it means
the sentence of reasoning that explains why a piece of evidence supports a claim
in Jewish law, the thirty-nine categories of work that the Mishnah lists as forbidden on the Sabbath

look.title: The Second Reason for the Sabbath

look.prompt: Write a warrant that connects this verse to the claim that the Torah treats rest as owed to the vulnerable.

check.q: What are the three layers of evidence named in the lesson?
choices: The thesis, the body and the conclusion
The quoted text, its context, and how adherents have read it
The author, the date and the publisher
The claim, the counterclaim and the rebuttal
check.why: Evidence starts with the text, adds genre and setting, and then adds the community's reading of the passage.

check.q: According to the lesson, what does the Mishnah list about the Sabbath?
choices: The seven days of creation
The names of the prophets who kept it
Thirty-nine categories of forbidden work
The prayers said in the Temple
check.why: The Mishnah, compiled about 200 CE, lists thirty-nine categories of work, the melakhot, forbidden on the Sabbath.

check.q: What is a warrant?
choices: The reasoning that explains why the evidence supports the claim
A quotation longer than three lines
A citation of the translation used
A secondary source that agrees with the thesis
check.why: The warrant joins text, context and reading to the claim so the reader does not have to guess how they connect.

lessons.title: Diversity Within a Tradition
lessons.mainIdea: Every tradition speaks with many voices, so a strong paper names the branch or school it means and reports where members disagree.
reading: On a Friday evening in Skokie, two Jewish families sit down to Sabbath dinner. In the first, an Orthodox family, no one will drive, cook or switch on a light until Saturday night, and in the morning they will walk to synagogue. In the second, a Reform family, candles are lit and the blessing is said over wine and bread. The next morning they drive to temple and spend the afternoon together, but they do not follow the full set of Sabbath rules. Both families are keeping the Sabbath, in the ways their movements teach.

Judaism today has several *branches*, organized movements with their own teachers and institutions. Orthodox Judaism holds that Jewish law remains binding in full. Conservative Judaism holds that the law is binding but has developed over time. Reform Judaism treats the law as a guide that each generation and each person may interpret. A paper that says Jews rest on the Sabbath by not switching on lights has described one branch and called it the whole. A paper that says many Orthodox Jews do not switch electrical devices on or off on the Sabbath, while Reform Judaism stresses rest and family, has described the tradition.

The same is true everywhere in the course. Hindu teachers have read the Gita in different ways. Shankara read it as a path of knowledge, Ramanuja as a path of devotion, and Gandhi as a guide to selfless action. Confucian thinkers also disagreed. Mencius held that human nature is good and needs nurturing. Xunzi held that it tends toward selfishness and needs shaping by ritual. These are *schools of thought*, lines of interpretation inside one tradition, and a capstone should name them when they bear on the question.

Disagreement inside a tradition is not a sign that its members are confused or inconsistent. It is what happens when many people, across centuries, take the same texts seriously. Report it the way you report any teaching, with attribution. Write most and many where the evidence supports them, and name who holds the minority view. Do not quietly choose the branch that fits your thesis best and present it as the only one. A reader from that tradition would notice, and so would the rubric.

words.d: an organized movement within a tradition, with its own teachers and institutions, such as Orthodox or Reform Judaism
the branch of Judaism that holds Jewish law to be binding in full, as developed in rabbinic tradition
the branch of Judaism that treats Jewish law as a guide each generation and person may interpret
a line of interpretation within a tradition, such as the followers of Mencius or of Xunzi in Confucianism

look.title: Two Tables, One Sabbath
look.text: Table one: candles lit before sunset, no cooking after, no car in the morning, a long walk to synagogue, the day ending with the Havdalah blessing at nightfall. Table two: candles and blessings over wine and bread, a family dinner, a drive to temple on Saturday morning, an afternoon with no work email. Both families say they are keeping the Sabbath.

check.q: How does Conservative Judaism differ from Orthodox Judaism, according to the lesson?
choices: Conservative Judaism does not observe the Sabbath
Conservative Judaism rejects the Torah
Conservative Judaism has no rabbis
Conservative Judaism holds that the law is binding but has developed over time
check.why: Orthodox Judaism holds the law binding in full; Conservative Judaism holds it binding but developing; Reform treats it as a guide.

check.q: Mencius and Xunzi disagreed about what?
choices: Whether human nature is good or tends toward selfishness
Whether the Analects should be written down
Whether the Gita is about knowledge or devotion
Whether the Sabbath overrides saving a life

check.q: What does the lesson say about disagreement within a tradition?
choices: It shows that members are confused
It should be left out to keep the thesis simple

It means the tradition has no real teaching
check.why: The lesson treats internal disagreement as normal and asks for attribution, qualifiers and names of the schools.

lessons.title: Comparing Without Ranking
lessons.mainIdea: Comparison sets traditions side by side to show where they agree and differ; ranking judges which is best, and the capstone does only the first.
reading: Maya builds a table before she writes her comparison section. Across the top are her three traditions. Down the side are four rows: who is owed rest, who owes it, how often, and why. In the Torah column she writes: the whole household; the head of the household; every seventh day; God's command and the memory of Egypt. In the Gita column: the self; the self; daily, in balance; discipline that ends sorrow. In the Analects column: the people; the ruler; by the seasons; a ruler's virtue. The table makes the pattern visible at a glance.

A *comparison* shows likeness and difference. A *parallel* is a point where two traditions answer in a similar way: both the Torah and the Analects place a duty on someone with power over others. A *contrast* is a point where they differ: the Torah sets a fixed day, while the Analects speak of fitting seasons. Good comparison names both, and then asks why. Here, one answer is that the Torah's command comes as law to a whole people, while the Analects offer advice to rulers.

*Ranking* is different. It judges which tradition is better, truer, wiser or more advanced. The capstone does not rank, for two reasons. No text can settle which tradition is right, so a ranking would rest on opinion, not evidence. And a public school studies religion without favoring or opposing any faith. Watch for ranking words: better, higher, more rational, primitive, superstitious. Watch too for hidden ranking, which uses one tradition as the measuring stick. To say the Analects lack a Sabbath is to measure Confucianism by Judaism.

The opposite mistake is just as unfair. To say all three traditions really teach the same thing about rest is not generous. It erases the differences their adherents care about. A Jew who keeps the Sabbath and a Hindu who practices yoga are not doing the same thing, and neither would want the difference hidden. Fair comparison keeps each tradition's answer in its own terms. It then shows exactly where the answers meet and where they part.

words.d: setting two or more traditions side by side to show where they agree and where they differ
a point where two traditions answer a question in a similar way
a point where two traditions answer a question differently
judging which tradition is better or truer, which the academic study of religion does not do

look.title: Two Comparison Sentences
look.text: Sentence A: Unlike Judaism, Confucianism never developed a proper day of rest, so its view of work is less humane. Sentence B: The Torah sets a fixed weekly day of rest for the whole household, while the Analects ask a ruler to call on the people's labor only at fitting seasons; both place a duty on those with power over others.
look.prompt: Find the ranking and the hidden measuring stick in Sentence A. Then name the parallel and the contrast in Sentence B.

check.q: In Maya's table, what is one parallel between the Torah and the Analects?
choices: Both set a fixed weekly day of rest
Both place the duty on the self alone
Both describe rest as a way to end sorrow
Both place a duty on someone with power over others
check.why: The head of the household in the Torah and the ruler in the Analects each owe rest to those under them.

check.q: Why does the phrase the Analects lack a Sabbath count as hidden ranking?
choices: It measures Confucianism by Judaism's standard
It misquotes the Analects
It uses a word that is not in the Analects
It ranks the Analects above the Torah
check.why: Hidden ranking uses one tradition as the measuring stick. Better: say where the Analects place the duty, in their own terms.

check.q: Why is saying all three traditions teach the same thing about rest a problem?
choices: Because it ranks them
Because it erases differences their adherents care about
Because it quotes too many texts
Because the rubric forbids the word same
check.why: Fair comparison keeps each answer in its own terms; flattening them into sameness misrepresents all three.

lessons.title: Respectful Language
lessons.mainIdea: Use each tradition's own names and terms, attribute every belief, and replace loaded words with accurate, neutral ones.
reading: Compare two sentences. God commanded the Israelites to rest on the seventh day. In the Torah, God commands the Israelites to rest on the seventh day. The first states a religious claim as fact. The second reports what a text says. In a public-school paper the second is correct every time, whatever the writer personally believes. *Attribution*, naming whose belief or text a statement comes from, is the most important habit of respectful language, and it costs only a few words: Muslims hold, according to the Gita, in Sikh teaching.

Use the names traditions use for themselves. Older English books sometimes called Muslims Mohammedans, a term Muslims reject because it suggests they worship Muhammad. The Hebrew Bible is called the *Tanakh* in Jewish tradition and the Old Testament in Christian tradition. Choose the term that fits your sentence, and know why the names differ. Sikhs regard the Guru Granth Sahib as their living Guru, so the name is always given in full. Many academic writers use BCE and CE for dates because the labels do not assume any faith.

Some words carry a judgment inside them. A *loaded word* sounds descriptive but ranks or mocks. Cult, when used for a small or new religious group, implies it is dangerous or false. Myth, when used to mean a false story, dismisses a sacred narrative. Primitive calls an oral tradition backward. Idol worship describes Hindu practice from outside and with scorn. A *murti* is a sacred image in which many Hindus understand the deity to be present. Use that word, with its gloss, instead.

Respect does not mean praise or silence. You may describe hard texts, conflicts and disagreements, including your own reservations if the assignment invites them, as long as you describe them accurately and attribute them. Respect means that a thoughtful member of the tradition could read your sentence and say: yes, that is what we hold, and that is how we would put it. That is the test. Read your draft once more with a member of each tradition in mind before you turn it in.

words.d: naming whose belief or text a statement comes from, as in according to the Qur'an or many Buddhists hold
the Jewish name for the Hebrew Bible, formed from the first letters of its three parts: Torah, Prophets and Writings
a word that sounds descriptive but carries a judgment, such as primitive or cult
in Hindu practice, a sacred image in which many Hindus understand the deity to be present

look.title: Revise the Sentence

Problems to find: a loaded word, a missing term from the tradition itself, and a flat description of the Guru Granth Sahib that leaves out how Sikhs themselves regard it. Each can be fixed in a few words.
look.prompt: Rewrite the draft so that a thoughtful Hindu and a thoughtful Sikh would each recognize their own practice in it.

check.q: Which sentence uses attribution correctly?
choices: God commanded the Israelites to rest
Everyone knows God commanded rest
In the Torah, God commands the Israelites to rest
Rest was commanded by the true God
check.why: It reports what a text says rather than stating a religious claim as fact, which is the rule in a public-school paper.

check.q: Why do Muslims reject the old term Mohammedan?
choices: It suggests they worship Muhammad
It refers only to Shia Muslims
It is an Arabic word for unbeliever
It was used only in the Qur'an
check.why: Muslims worship God alone and regard Muhammad as a prophet, so a name built on his suggests something they reject.

check.q: What is the lesson's test for respectful language?
choices: The sentence praises every tradition
The sentence avoids any mention of disagreement
The sentence uses the longest term available
A thoughtful member of the tradition would recognize the description as accurate
check.why: Respect does not mean praise or silence; it means accurate, attributed description that adherents would recognize.

lessons.title: Handling Difficult Texts
lessons.mainIdea: When a text speaks of war, punishment or unequal roles, quote it accurately, give its context, and report how adherents have read it, without attacking or excusing.
reading: Every scripture in this course contains passages that trouble some readers. The Gita is spoken on a battlefield, where Krishna urges Arjuna to fight. The Hebrew Bible contains laws of war. The Qur'an contains verses about fighting. Early Christian letters give instructions about slaves and wives that many readers today find hard. A capstone question about war, family or forgiveness will lead you to such passages. The worst choices are to skip them, which misrepresents the text, or to use them as weapons, which misrepresents the tradition.

Treat a difficult text exactly like any other: text, context, reading. Take Qur'an 2:190, which tells believers to fight those who fight them but not to overstep limits. The *historical context*, as Muslim tradition presents it, is the conflict between the early Muslim community at Medina and its opponents from Mecca. Many Muslim scholars have read the verse as permitting fighting in defense and within limits. Interpretations have varied across fourteen centuries and among legal schools. Your paper can say all of that in four sentences, each attributed.

Readings of the Gita show how much interpretation matters. Some Hindu commentators read the battle as real and teach that a warrior's duty, his *dharma*, required him to fight. Gandhi, who practiced nonviolence, read the battlefield as an *allegory*, a story in which the fighting stands for the inner struggle between right and wrong. Both readings come from within the tradition. A paper on war that quotes Krishna's command without these readings has told half the story.

Two cautions keep a paper fair. Do not apologize for a tradition by hiding a hard verse, and do not prosecute it by quoting that verse alone. Also keep the text separate from the history. What a scripture says and what some members did in its name are different questions, and each needs its own evidence and dates. Describe violence, persecution and conflict factually, with places and dates, and let the reader weigh them.

words.d: the time, place and events surrounding a text, as the tradition and historians describe them
a story in which characters and events stand for ideas, such as a battle standing for an inner struggle
in Hindu tradition, duty and the right way to live, which differs with a person's role and stage of life

look.title: Fighting and Its Limits
look.text: The Qur'an tells believers to fight, in the way of God, those who fight against them, but not to go beyond the limits, because God does not love those who overstep them.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:190, paraphrased from the standard text
look.prompt: Write the context and reading layers for this verse in two attributed sentences, using the lesson's information.

check.q: According to the lesson, what are the two worst ways to handle a difficult text?
choices: Quoting it and citing it
Skipping it, or using it alone as a weapon
Giving its context and its reading
Naming its genre and its translator
check.why: Skipping a hard text misrepresents the scripture; quoting it alone as a weapon misrepresents the tradition.

check.q: How did Gandhi read the battlefield of the Gita?
choices: As a record of a battle he wanted repeated
As a law for all soldiers
As an allegory of the inner struggle between right and wrong
As a later addition to be ignored
check.why: Gandhi, who practiced nonviolence, read the battle as an allegory, while other Hindu commentators read it as a warrior's real duty.

check.q: Why does the lesson say to keep the text separate from the history?
choices: Because history is not part of the study of religion
Because texts have no dates
Because the rubric counts only texts
Because what a scripture says and what some members did in its name are different questions needing their own evidence
check.why: Each question needs its own evidence and dates; merging them misrepresents both the text and the people.

lessons.title: Building the Written Essay
lessons.mainIdea: The essay moves from the question to the thesis, gives each tradition its own section of layered evidence, then compares them and names the limits of the study.
reading: The written essay has five parts, in order. The *introduction* poses the question, explains in a sentence or two why it matters, and ends with the thesis. Next come three body sections, one for each tradition. Each section follows the five moves from earlier in this chapter: claim, text, context, reading and warrant. Then comes a comparison section that sets the three answers side by side. The conclusion states the answer again in fresh words and names what the study could not settle. Last is a works-cited list with full information for every translation and secondary source.

There are two ways to organize a comparison. In *block structure*, you finish one tradition before starting the next, then compare at the end. It is easier to write, and it keeps each tradition's answer whole. In *point-by-point structure*, each section takes one row of the comparison table, such as who is owed rest, and answers it for all three traditions at once. It makes the comparison sharper but can break up each tradition's voice. Many strong capstones use block structure for the body and point-by-point structure for the comparison section.

The comparison section is where the thesis is proved, and it is the part students most often rush. Walk the reader through each parallel and each contrast. Then give your best explanation for the pattern, grounded in genre and context. Maya might explain that the Torah speaks as law to a people, the Gita as teaching to one person, and the Analects as advice to rulers. So each locates the duty of rest where its own genre points: the community, the self or the state.

The conclusion should name the study's *limits*. Maya read the Gita in English, not Sanskrit. She used three passages from traditions with thousands of pages. She interviewed one family from one branch of Judaism. Naming limits does not weaken a paper. It tells the reader exactly how far the evidence reaches, and that is a mark of honest scholarship. End with the question the study opened but could not answer. For Maya, it is how each tradition would speak to a modern worker's schedule.

words.d: the opening of an essay, which poses the question, explains why it matters and ends with the thesis
an essay organization that discusses one tradition completely before moving to the next
an essay organization that answers one part of the question for all traditions before moving to the next part
the boundaries of what a study's evidence can show, such as reading in translation or using a few passages

look.cite: Suggested plan for a capstone essay of about 2,300 words, following Maya's three traditions
look.prompt: The comparison section gets the largest share. Using the lesson, explain why, and say what would go wrong if it got only 100 words.

check.q: What does the introduction of the capstone essay end with?
choices: The thesis
The works-cited list
The longest quotation
The limits of the study
check.why: The introduction poses the question, explains why it matters, and ends with the thesis the essay will prove.

check.q: What is point-by-point structure?
choices: Finishing one tradition before starting the next
Quoting one verse per paragraph
Answering one part of the question for all traditions before moving to the next part
Listing every point in the introduction
check.why: Point-by-point structure takes one row of the comparison table at a time, which sharpens the comparison.

check.q: Why does the lesson say naming limits does not weaken a paper?
choices: Because teachers do not read the conclusion
Because it tells the reader exactly how far the evidence reaches

lessons.title: The Oral Presentation
lessons.mainIdea: A strong presentation states the thesis early, reads one key text per tradition accurately with its citation, and treats sacred words and objects with care.
reading: A listener cannot flip back a page. That one fact shapes every choice in an *oral presentation*. State the question and thesis in the first minute and show the thesis on screen. Use *signposts*, spoken markers that tell listeners where they are, such as: that was the Torah's answer; now the Gita's. Give each tradition one key passage, not five. Put the quotation on a slide with the citation and translation beneath it. Then read it aloud slowly, exactly as printed.

Reading a sacred text aloud is a responsibility. Practice every name and term until you can say it without stumbling: Bhagavad Gita, Analects, Guru Granth Sahib, Tanakh. If you are unsure of a pronunciation, ask your teacher or a member of the tradition, not a guess from spelling. Say the translation aloud as well: in the King James translation, or in a paraphrase of chapter 6 of the Gita. Your listeners should always know whose words they are hearing.

Visual aids help when they carry information. A photograph of a Sabbath table, a map of where the Analects were compiled, or a comparison table can all teach. Some images need care. Many Muslims avoid any picture of the Prophet Muhammad, so a presentation should not show one. Physical scriptures also need care. Sikhs keep the Guru Granth Sahib covered on a raised platform, and many Muslims handle a copy of the Qur'an only in a state of ritual cleanliness. A printed excerpt is usually the respectful choice for a classroom.

Do not perform another tradition's ritual or wear its religious clothing as a costume. You may describe a ritual, show a respectful photograph, or play a recording made and shared by the community. The line is between showing how adherents practice and imitating it for effect. Close the presentation by returning to the thesis in one sentence. Then invite questions, which the next lesson takes up.
